[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim T_{n-1}]

where [MATH: T_{n-1}] is a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n=9] drawn from a normal population. The sample mean is [MATH: \overline{x}=30,] and the sample standard deviation is [MATH: s=3.3.]
We wish to compute a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu.]

Content:
Recall that a confidence interval is an interval of the form

Content:
[MATH: (\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E),]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \overline{x}] is an estimate of the population mean, and
- [MATH: E] is the margin of error.

Content:
In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] is also normally distributed, where

Content:
[MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Content:
By transforming [MATH: \overline{X}] in the manner described earlier, we have that the random variable [MATH: T,] defined as

Content:
[MATH: T = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n},]

Content:
follows a student's [MATH: t]-distribution [MATH: T_{n-1}] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
We wish to find a [MATH: t]-interval that we're [MATH: 95\%] confident that the random variable [MATH: T] lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a49488fa3e6edd131fec08fdad68f5ff]

Content:
Since we wish to find a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval, we define our parameter [MATH: \alpha] as

Content:
[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as [MATH: \pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2}\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b4e797c88928f5c0ad1b610061411642]

Content:
According to our diagram,

Content:
[MATH: P(T > t_{8,0.025}) = P(T < -t_{8,0.025}) = 0.025.]

Content:
Using a table of values for the [MATH: t]-distribution, we find that [MATH: t_{8,0.025} \approx 2.306.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: P(T > 2.306) = P(T < -2.306) = 0.025.]

Content:
In other words,

Content:
[MATH: P(− 2.306 < T < 2.306) = 0.95]

Content:
Therefore, there is a [MATH: 95\%] probability that our random variable [MATH: T] will lie in the interval [MATH: (-2.306, 2.306).]

Content:
Similar to the case where [MATH: \sigma^2] was known, we find the appropriate confidence interval by solving the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean [MATH: \mu\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: − 2.306|< T < 2.306; − 2.306|< (x^(―) − μ)/(s/sqrt(n)) < 2.306; − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|< x^(―) − μ < 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)); − x^(―) − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|< − μ < − x^(―) + 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)); x^(―) + 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|> μ > x^(―) − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)); x^(―) − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|< μ < x^(―) + 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))]

Content:
Therefore, a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(\overline{x}-2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x}+2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \right).]

Content:
Finally, substituting our values

Content:
[MATH: n=9, \qquad
\overline{x}=30, \qquad
s=3.3,]

Content:
we obtain that our [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for [MATH: \mu] is

Content:
[MATH: \big( 30- 2.537, \: 30 + 2.537 \big).]

Content:
Describing this confidence interval using confidence limits, we have

Content:
[MATH: 30 \pm 2.537.]

Content:
Let's now describe the general procedure.

Consider a sample of size [MATH: n=9] from a normal population. Given that the sample mean is [MATH: 50] and the sample standard deviation is [MATH: 1.5,] find a [MATH: 99\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] of the distribution.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that the population is normally distributed, but we do not know the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

In cases like this, the random variable

[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n}]

follows a student's [MATH: t]-distribution [MATH: T_{n-1}] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom, where

  • [MATH: \overline{X}] is the sample mean,

  • [MATH: \mu] is the population mean,

  • [MATH: S^2] is the sample variance, and

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

[MATH: \overline{x} \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}},]

where [MATH: P(T > t_{n-1,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] and [MATH: T] has a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

In our case,

[MATH: \overline{x}=50, \qquad n = 9, \qquad s = 1.5.]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 99\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.99=0.01 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.005.]

We are given that [MATH: P(T > 3.355) = 0.005.] As a result,

[MATH: t_{n-1,\alpha/2} = t_{8,0.005} = 3.355.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 99\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is the following:

[MATH: 50|± 3.355 ⋅ (1.5)/(sqrt(9)); 50|± 1.678]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n] drawn from a normal population with unknown population mean [MATH: \mu] and known population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Recall that a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{x}] is the sample mean, [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
One thing to realize is that this situation is unrealistic: it's doubtful that we'll not know the population mean yet know the population variance.

Content:
A more realistic situation is that [MATH: \sigma^2] is unknown, and we must estimate it using the sample data. To estimate the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2,] we use the sample variance [MATH: S^2,] given by

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2.]

Content:
It can be shown that
[MATH: \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim T_{n-1}]

Content:
where [MATH: T_{n-1}] is a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
Let's take a look at a concrete example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Constructing Confidence Intervals

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n=9] drawn from a normal population. The sample mean is [MATH: \overline{x}=30,] and the sample standard deviation is [MATH: s=3.3.]
We wish to compute a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu.]

Content:
Recall that a confidence interval is an interval of the form

Content:
[MATH: (\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E),]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \overline{x}] is an estimate of the population mean, and
- [MATH: E] is the margin of error.

Content:
In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] is also normally distributed, where

Content:
[MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Content:
By transforming [MATH: \overline{X}] in the manner described earlier, we have that the random variable [MATH: T,] defined as

Content:
[MATH: T = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt n},]

Content:
follows a student's [MATH: t]-distribution [MATH: T_{n-1}] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
We wish to find a [MATH: t]-interval that we're [MATH: 95\%] confident that the random variable [MATH: T] lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a49488fa3e6edd131fec08fdad68f5ff]

Content:
Since we wish to find a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval, we define our parameter [MATH: \alpha] as

Content:
[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as [MATH: \pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2}\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b4e797c88928f5c0ad1b610061411642]

Content:
According to our diagram,

Content:
[MATH: P(T > t_{8,0.025}) = P(T < -t_{8,0.025}) = 0.025.]

Content:
Using a table of values for the [MATH: t]-distribution, we find that [MATH: t_{8,0.025} \approx 2.306.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: P(T > 2.306) = P(T < -2.306) = 0.025.]

Content:
In other words,

Content:
[MATH: P(− 2.306 < T < 2.306) = 0.95]

Content:
Therefore, there is a [MATH: 95\%] probability that our random variable [MATH: T] will lie in the interval [MATH: (-2.306, 2.306).]

Content:
Similar to the case where [MATH: \sigma^2] was known, we find the appropriate confidence interval by solving the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean [MATH: \mu\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: − 2.306|< T < 2.306; − 2.306|< (x^(―) − μ)/(s/sqrt(n)) < 2.306; − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|< x^(―) − μ < 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)); − x^(―) − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|< − μ < − x^(―) + 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)); x^(―) + 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|> μ > x^(―) − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)); x^(―) − 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))|< μ < x^(―) + 2.306 ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n))]

Content:
Therefore, a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(\overline{x}-2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x}+2.306 \cdot\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \right).]

Content:
Finally, substituting our values

Content:
[MATH: n=9, \qquad
\overline{x}=30, \qquad
s=3.3,]

Content:
we obtain that our [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for [MATH: \mu] is

Content:
[MATH: \big( 30- 2.537, \: 30 + 2.537 \big).]

Content:
Describing this confidence interval using confidence limits, we have

Content:
[MATH: 30 \pm 2.537.]

Content:
Let's now describe the general procedure.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Unknown Population Variance

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a normal population with the unknown population mean [MATH: \mu] and sample variance [MATH: s^2.] Then, for a given value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population mean [MATH: \mu] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(\overline{x} - t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} +t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)]

Content:
where [MATH: P(T > t_{n-1, \alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] and [MATH: T \sim T_{n-1}.]

Content:
The endpoints of our confidence interval are called confidence limits and are given by

Content:
[MATH: \overline{x} \pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.]

Content:
Each part of the formula above has a name:

Content:
- [MATH: \overline{x}] is an estimate of the population mean
- [MATH: \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}] is the standard error of the mean
- [MATH: t_{n-1,\alpha/2}] is the corresponding [MATH: t]-score
- [MATH: E = t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}] is the margin of error

Content:
[MATH: t]

Content:
So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (x^(―) − [margin of error],|x^(―) + [margin of error]); (x^(―) − [[math]t[/math]-score] ⋅ [standard error],|x^(―) + [[math]t[/math]-score] ⋅ [standard error]); (x^(―) − t_{n − 1, α/2} ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)),|x^(―) + t_{n − 1, α/2} ⋅ (s)/(sqrt(n)))]

Content:
Notice that the expression for the confidence interval is very similar to when the population variance was known. The only difference is that we now use the [MATH: t]-scores instead of [MATH: z]-scores and the sample standard deviation [MATH: s] instead of the population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma.]

Content:
Finally, since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably.

---

Item 4 — Example: Finding Confidence Intervals From Normal Populations

Example Prompt:

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(T > 3.355) = 0.005,] where [MATH: T] has a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: 8] degrees of freedom.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
